name: Henry Paulson

summary.text: Henry M. Paulson Jr. was chairman and chief executive of Goldman Sachs from 1999 to 2006 and served as the 74th United States Secretary of the Treasury from July 2006 to January 2009, during the 2008 financial crisis. In November 2011 Bloomberg Markets reported that on July 21, 2008 he met a group of hedge-fund managers at Eton Park Capital Management in Manhattan and described a possible scenario for placing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship, seven weeks before that happened. Paulson declined to comment on the report; Bloomberg said it found no evidence that attendees traded on the information. He is the founder and chairman of the Paulson Institute.

facts.claim: Paulson spent 32 years at Goldman Sachs, serving as co-chairman and co-CEO in 1998 and as chairman and CEO from 1999 until 2006.

facts.claim: Paulson was nominated by President George W. Bush on May 30, 2006 to succeed John Snow as the 74th Secretary of the Treasury and was sworn in on July 10, 2006, serving until January 2009.
facts.quote: He was sworn in on July 10, 2006, with Chief Justice Roberts administering the oath while President Bush looked on.

facts.claim: On taking office in 2006, Paulson sold his Goldman Sachs holdings, reported as 3.23 million shares, to comply with federal conflict-of-interest rules; unvested stock options were also to be sold. Under a 1989 ethics law an appointee may obtain a certificate of divestiture that defers capital-gains tax if the proceeds are reinvested in approved assets.
facts.quote: A spokeswoman said Paulson is making the sale in order to conform with federal conflict-of-interest rules.

facts.claim: Bloomberg Markets reported in November 2011 that on July 21, 2008 Paulson visited the Third Avenue offices of hedge fund Eton Park Capital Management in Manhattan, where around a dozen hedge-fund managers and other Wall Street executives were gathered, at least five of them Goldman Sachs alumni.
facts.quote: Around the conference room table were a dozen or so hedge-fund managers and other Wall Street executives -- at least five of them alumni of Goldman Sachs Group Inc., of which Paulson was chief executive officer and chairman from 1999 to 2006.

sources.title: How Paulson Gave Hedge Funds Advance Word of Fannie Rescue
Henry Paulson alerted hedge funds in advance to Fannie, Freddie rescue

facts.claim: According to a fund manager who attended, Bloomberg reported, Paulson described at the Eton Park meeting a possible scenario for placing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship, a government seizure that would let the firms continue operating; the same morning he had told New York Times reporters that a Fed and OCC examination of the companies' books would give a signal of confidence to the markets.
facts.quote: According to an attendee, Paulson described a possible scenario for placing Fannie and Freddie into "conservatorship" — a government seizure designed to allow the firms to continue operations despite heavy losses in the mortgage markets. Seven weeks later, the government did exactly that.

facts.claim: Bloomberg reported that it found no evidence attendees traded on what they heard, noting that firm-specific short stock sales cannot be tracked using public documents; law professors quoted said Paulson was under no legal obligation not to share material nonpublic information in his role as Treasury Secretary.
facts.quote: Bloomberg's reporting said there was no evidence that they did so after the meeting; tracking firm-specific short stock sales isn't possible using public documents.

facts.claim: Paulson declined to comment on the Bloomberg report through a spokeswoman; the other executives known to have attended also declined to comment. A spokesman for Blackstone, owner of attendee Bennett Goodman's GSO Capital Partners, said the firm did not believe market-sensitive information was discussed.
facts.quote: Paulson, now a distinguished senior fellow at the University of Chicago, declined to comment through a spokeswoman.

facts.claim: On September 7, 2008, Treasury announced that the Federal Housing Finance Agency had placed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship and that Treasury had entered Preferred Stock Purchase Agreements committing it to keep each company's net worth positive in exchange for senior preferred shares and warrants; existing common and preferred shareholders absorb losses before the government's senior preferred shares. FHFA's history page dates the conservatorship decision to September 6, 2008.
facts.quote: Treasury commits to keeping each company's net worth positive, and in exchange it receives senior preferred shares and warrants.

sources.title: Statement by Secretary Henry M. Paulson, Jr. on Treasury and Federal Housing Finance Agency Action to Protect Financial Markets and Taxpayers
History of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Conservatorships

facts.claim: In his September 7, 2008 statement Paulson said he had concluded that a direct Treasury equity investment in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in their existing form would not have served taxpayers.
facts.quote: it would not have been in the best interest of the taxpayers for Treasury to simply make an equity investment in these enterprises in their current form

openQuestions: The Bloomberg article's full text could not be opened in this session; the quotes come from the search excerpt and from syndicated copies (Seattle Times, Financial Advisor, NPR). The owner should confirm the wording against bloomberg.com.

No statement from Eton Park or Eric Mindich on the meeting or on any Fannie/Freddie trading was found; Bloomberg's reporting says attendees declined to comment and that no evidence of trading was found. The site's claim that attendees 'captured billions' shorting the GSEs is not supported by any source found.

Sources disagree on whether the 2006 certificate of divestiture made Paulson's Goldman sale tax-free or only deferred the tax; the New York Sun describes deferral. The $200 million tax-saving figure circulating online comes from a weak source and was not recorded.

The site says Paulson told Congress that day the GSEs were well capitalized; the sources found describe New York Times remarks that morning and Senate testimony days earlier, not congressional testimony on July 21 itself.
